newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Clinton calls for united Europe.
newsitem.headline: Clinton calls for united Europe.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton, celebrating the Marshall Plan that helped rebuild Western Europe from the ashes of World War Two, called on the West on Wednesday to forge a united Europe with the former Soviet bloc.

In an address to European leaders gathered to mark the 50th anniversary of the plan, which was proposed in 1947 by then U.S. Secretary of State George Marshall, Clinton also pledged that the United States would never abandon the continent.

"We must summon the spirit of the Marshall Plan for the next 50 years and beyond to build a Europe that is democratic, at peace and undivided for the first time in history," Clinton said in a speech at the Binnenhof palace in The Hague.

"Today I affirm to the people of Europe, as General Marshall did 50 years ago: America stands with you," he said. "We have learned the lessons of history. We will not walk away. No less than five decades ago, our destinies are joined."

Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, who hosted the celebration in the Dutch capitol, offered thanks for the 16 countries that benefited from the plan, which pumped $13 billion, an estimated $88 billion in today's money, into their shattered economies.

"Through you Mr. President, I thank the American people on behalf of all the Marshall countries for their generous support at such a critical moment in history," Kok said. "You made a vital difference."
The ceremony, held in one of the Netherlands' elegant royal palaces, brought tears to the eyes of German Chancellor Helmut kohl, who was among the leaders gathered for the celebration.

Clinton travelled to Europe this week for a series of events to commemorate the Marshall Plan and to grapple with the effort to integrate Russia and the former Soviet satellites of Eastern and Central Europe more closely with the West.

In Paris on Tuesday, he signed a historic agreement with Russian President Boris Yeltsin and the leaders of the other NATO countries to tighten Moscow's relationship with the 16-nation Western security alliance, its former enemy.

Clinton suggested NATO was one of many instruments to bind together the continent, divided by the end of World War Two. "Through NATO ... we can do for Europe's east what we did for Europe's west -- defend freedom, strengthen democracy, temper old rivalries, hasten integration and provide a stable climate in which prosperity can grow," he said.

And at a twice-yearly summit with European Union leaders in The Hague earlier on Wednesday, Clinton said more private investment needed to be pumped into east Europe's ex-communist states to build on already substantial aid from the West.
Following the summit, Clinton, Kok and European Commission President Jacques Santer stopped short of announcing a second Marshall Plan, but urged greater efforts at integration.
"We can't simply say to those countries (in eastern Europe) 'We want you to be free democracies, we want you to have economic reform and good luck'," Clinton said at a news conference.

Noting that a more prosperous and united Europe would be a stronger partner for the U.S., Clinton was non-committal on plans for European monetary union, saying only that European integration was good for all.
"We are not only not threatened by that, we are excited about it, he said.
But he said it would be inappropriate for him to comment on the mechanics of a single currency: "The decision to do that and the mechanics (of it) are a matter for the Union," he said.

Clinton, accompanied by his wife Hillary, brought tight security to The Hague but delighted onlookers with an impromptu 10-minute canalside walk-about at midday and then by window shopping in the city centre with his wife in the afternoon.
Later on Wednesday, he was scheduled to attend an open-air celebration of the Marshall Plan at the port city of Rotterdam.

The president's trip was, however, overshadowed by a U.S. Supreme Court decision on Tuesday to let a sexual harassment lawsuit brought against him by Paula Jones go ahead rather than allowing it to be heard after he leaves office in 2001.
Clinton declined to comment on his own case, but suggested that the decision might set a difficult precedent for future presidents who might have to face such suits while in office.

"As to what might happen to future presidents, I am concerned about that but there may not be anything to be done about that. The Supreme Court has made its decision," Clinton told reporters in his first public comment on the ruling.
